The proof uses matching-based local distributions, weighted induction, and convex separation to establish the edgewise cut guarantees while maintaining global balance.

papers.title: Instability of non-minimal critical points of Newton's equation with real analytic potentials
papers.abstract: We prove that any non-minimal critical point of a real analytic potential on a finite-dimensional Euclidean space possesses a nonconstant zero-energy Newton trajectory that converges to the equilibrium as \(t\to+\infty\). By time reversibility, this yields forward Lyapunov instability. We do not assume the critical point is isolated. The proof constructs angular minima via quadratic regularization, matching the regularization coefficient to the leading inertial term. A free forcing coefficient allows continuation past bounded accumulations of correction orders. For polynomial potentials, this produces a complete Hahn-series solution, and differential algebraicity gives a common Puiseux denominator. A fixed-denominator continuation estimate together with a finite Taylor transfer extends the construction to analytic potentials. The realization theorem for the resulting invariant formal phase curve then yields a genuine trajectory. We also exhibit an isolated polynomial singularity for which an exact Euler-field identity admits no relatively differentiable solution on the negative set of the potential.

papers.title: Exciton-polarons in monolayer semiconductors with drifting electrons
papers.abstract: Recent work has demonstrated that the optical absorption of moderately doped two-dimensional semiconductors can be described in terms of exciton-polarons. In this picture, interactions between a photoexcited exciton and a Fermi sea of excess charge carriers split the exciton spectrum into a lower-energy attractive polaron branch and a higher-energy repulsive polaron branch. Due to the negligible in-plane momentum of photons, however, optical measurements probe only exciton-polarons near zero momentum, leaving their finite-momentum physics largely unexplored. Here we propose accessing this regime by measuring the absorption in the presence of an electric bias current. In effect, this displaces the electronic Fermi sea in momentum space, such that an optically active exciton-polaron at rest acquires finite momentum relative to the charge carriers. Using a diagrammatic formulation of the exciton-polaron problem, we derive exact relations between the spectral and quasiparticle properties of current-biased exciton-polarons and their finite-momentum counterparts in an equilibrium Fermi sea. These relations show that absorption measurements with drifting electrons can reconstruct the momentum dependence of the quasiparticle properties for both branches. We estimate that experimentally accessible currents can probe a broad momentum range while remaining within the linear-response regime.

papers.title: Quantum Startup, Recoil Statistics and Collective Gain in Free-Electron Lasers
papers.abstract: We examine the conditions under which quantum signatures can be distinguished from classical dynamics and statistical fluctuations in a free-electron laser. Starting from minimal coupling and the Bambini--Renieri frame, we derive the momentum-photon exchange Hamiltonian and its Raman-Nath ladder. An interaction-picture expansion retains detuning exactly and organizes recoil corrections through the mismatch between neighboring orders. Its validity depends on the accumulated recoil phase over the populated ladder, rather than on elementary recoil alone. Numerical checks and Gaussian entrance packets illustrate the effects of preparation and resonance averaging. We distinguish number-state exchange amplitudes from predictions for a coherent optical seed, and joint electron-field coherence from reduced radiation coherence. The Wigner representation connects finite recoil translations with classical transport and identifies the information required for bunching. A cavity channel then provides the basis for comparison with the recoil-resolved oscillator proposed by Kling and Giese, including the optical-undulator preparation, stimulated back-action and narrow resonance acceptance. Space charge, spontaneous diffusion and FEL-induced energy spread are compared with recoil and high-gain bandwidth scales. The coherent undulator pump is essential to exclude artificial zero-recoil antibunching from a number-state preparation. Startup and excess photon variance alone do not establish a quantum signature: the specified observable must remain distinguishable from a classical stochastic baseline under compatible preparation, propagation and detection conditions.

papers.title: Free energy profile computations for force-induced melting of a short B-DNA using Jarzynski equality
papers.abstract: We initially equilibrate a system of solvated 12-base pair canonical B-DNA of a specified sequence in a state of no external force acting on it (state $A: f=0$). A switching experiment is then performed by pulling one end of the DNA while restraining its other end. The pulling force is taken up to a maximum of 400 pN (state $B$), at a specified constant rate. The non-equilibrium work done W associated with this finite-time process is determined by integrating the extension of the DNA molecule with respect to the applied force. The distribution of the work values $P(W)$ is obtained by repeating the pulling process several times, wherein each time, the process is started with macroscopic state $A$. The free energy profile $Φ(f)$ is obtained by a suitably devised method from the Jarzynski equality. The conformational space of the DNA is also sampled in an equilibrium method of umbrella sampling by considering the end-to-end length $ξ$ as the reaction coordinate. The associated potential of mean force (PMF) $Φ(ξ)$ is then computed by invoking the weighted histogram analysis method (WHAM). From the results, we observe that the equilibrium free energy difference between two states, $A$ and $B$, $ΔF_{AB} ~(=F_B -F_A)$ obtained through both methods, is in close agreement with each other, despite the differences along the profiles $Φ(f)$ and $Φ(ξ)$, attributed to their distinct pathways of unzipping.

papers.title: Large Language Model-based Optimization for Wireless Communication: A Survey
papers.abstract: The growing complexity and dynamism of modern wireless communication frameworks have made real-time optimization essential for efficient resource allocation. Traditional optimization and machine-learning techniques often struggle with generalization, adaptability, stability, and scalability in heterogeneous, time-varying environments. Large language models (LLMs) have recently emerged as powerful tools capable of reasoning over structured prompts and generating context-aware decisions in real time without domain-specific retraining. This survey provides a comprehensive review of LLM-driven optimization techniques applied to wireless communication problems such as power control, bandwidth allocation, task offloading, and intelligent surface configuration. We introduce a functional taxonomy of LLM-enabled wireless resource management strategies and analyze the prompt engineering methodologies employed in recent literature. Furthermore, we develop a generalized analytical framework that categorizes LLM-based optimization architectures, including direct solution generation, closed-loop optimization with external verifiers, and representation encoding within trainable neural pipelines. To demonstrate practical applicability, we present representative case studies on LLM-assisted beam prediction for millimeter-wave systems and adaptive wireless resource allocation. Finally, we discuss emerging hybrid AI approaches for wireless networks.

papers.title: Let Execution Do the Teaching
papers.abstract: Improving a coding model is a sequence of decisions: find the limiting behavior, create useful practice, and determine which attempts deserve reinforcement. We investigate a practical way to make those decisions increasingly repeatable by grounding feedback in execution. Starting from GLM-4.7-Flash, the work combines whole-file supervised fine-tuning, targeted C++ repair curricula, group-relative reinforcement learning, and verifiers that turn program behavior into structured rewards. Compiler errors and failing tests provide specific contexts for repair practice, while executable checks score the resulting programs. We evaluate the trained models on 26 C++ coding tasks, measuring both initial success and completion after test feedback. The strongest reported post-training configuration achieves 45.2% success in the first test round and 61.5% within two rounds. These results come from an assisted development suite with evolving prompt contracts; the strongest configuration uses four selected evaluation trials and includes six tasks also used in training. The study describes an execution-guided workflow for improving coding models, including how repair tasks are constructed, how program behavior determines rewards, and how the resulting models are evaluated.

papers.title: A Negative Answer to a Variant of the Lins-de Melo-Pugh Conjecture
papers.abstract: We study the polynomial Liénard system $$\dot x=y-(a_1x^{2m+1}+a_2x^{2n+1}+x^{2N}),\qquad \dot y=-x,$$ where $0\leq m< n<N$ are integers and $a_1a_2<0$. The supremum of the numbers of limit cycles in this family is at least two for every integer $N\geq3$ and at least three for $N=5$. These results disprove Conjectures 1.5 and 1.6 of Cen et al. [Sci. China Math. 69 (2026)].

papers.title: Uniqueness of limit cycle{s} in a class of classical trinomial Liénard systems
papers.abstract: This paper studies the number of limit cycles of the polynomial Liénard system $\dot x=y-F(x)$, $\dot y=-x$, where $F(x)=a_1x^{2N}+a_2x^{2m+1}+x^{2n+1}$, with integers \(N,m,n\) satisfying $2\le N\le m<n$, $a_1\ne0$ and $a_2\neq 0$. It is proved that this system has exactly one limit cycle and that every periodic orbit is hyperbolic and attracting for $a_2<0$; this system has no limit cycles for $a_2>0$. The uniqueness proof compares the widths and relative midpoints of the two scalar arcs obtained in potential coordinates. This result gives a positive answer to Conjecture 1.4 of Cen et al. (Sci. China Math., 2026).

papers.title: Who Writes the Codebook? An Eight-Step Framework for Auditing LLM-Generated Category Systems
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly create the categories through which qualitative evidence is interpreted. Existing coding benchmarks often hold these categories fixed. We propose the Qualitative Variance Audit Framework, an eight-step method that compares codebook creation, repeated application and code distributions under controlled inputs. It combines model-owned and shared-reference codebooks to distinguish variation in the overall pipeline from application differences within a common category system. An application to 668 organisational interviews, 13,166 text units and eight models from five vendors yields 48 codebooks and 270 coding runs. Models create markedly different category structures; mean within-model reliability ranges from .76 to .92, whereas between-model agreement on the shared codebook is about .69. The framework complements LLM-assisted grounded theory by exposing model dependencies before substantive interpretation. It assesses reliability and representational consequences, not interpretive validity or the quality of resulting theory.

papers.title: Interactive Structured Environment Scaling for Large Language Model Agentic Reasoning
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning via environmental interaction is a cornerstone post-training paradigm for evolving large language models into autonomous agents capable of multi-turn tool use and exploration. Because the environment defines what the policy observes and how actions are verified, its structure directly bounds the capabilities an agent can acquire. Yet existing structured and retrieval environments rely on upstream pre-filtering---extracting a compact subgraph around the gold answer or retrieving fixed passages before the policy acts. We show that such pre-filtering introduces a fundamental measurement confound: because per-question subgraphs enclose ground-truth paths, they compress the candidate space by orders of magnitude and leak answer locations via local topology, allowing a question-blind degree heuristic to surface gold answers far above chance. To restore path selection, candidate pruning, and optimal stopping as genuine policy decisions, we propose RISE (Interactive Structured Environment), which transitions structured reinforcement learning from static subgraphs to full-scale interactive databases along two coupled axes. First, Decision-Space Scaling exposes the unpruned knowledge graph via a five-stage graph-agnostic typed intent adapter under a bounded call budget and a multiplicative grounding reward gate. Second, Learning-Frontier Scaling overcomes within-group variance collapse under group-normalized objectives by uniting model-independent structural tier progression with a self-evolving competence-frontier bandit. Across nineteen benchmarks and three model backbones, RISE substantially advances in-domain and unseen-schema knowledge-graph reasoning, transfers zero-shot to open-domain passage retrieval, and significantly enhances out-of-domain mathematical and logical deduction.

papers.title: Toward an Admissibility Theory of Aharonov--Bohm Arbitrage
papers.abstract: This note develops a provisional admissibility framework for Aharonov-Bohm type arbitrage. Starting from a categorical filtration $F:\mathcal T_{\mathrm{mic}}^{\mathrm{op}}\to \mathsf{Prob}$ and its distortion on microscopic histories, we ask when a favorable closed microscopic loop can be realized as an executable relative ordinal arbitrage over an open macro-time interval. The history endofunctor $\mathsf{Hist}$ retains the staged decomposition of economic activities, while the twisted-arrow category $\operatorname{Tw}(\mathsf{Hist}(\mathcal T_{\mathrm{mic}}))$ represents a microscopic loop as an arrow between distinct histories. An observable clock $Π: \mathsf{Econ} \to \mathcal T_{\mathrm{mac}}$ and a microscopic realization functor $J: \mathsf{Hist}(\mathcal T_{\mathrm{mac}}) \to \operatorname{Tw}(\mathsf{Hist}(\mathcal T_{\mathrm{mic}}))$ connect economic histories with their microscopic geometry. Executability is treated separately through configuration histories, capacity constraints, observations, and policies. This yields pathwise and almost-sure notions of execution. A finite foreign-exchange model illustrates stochastic execution, capacity failure, terminal settlement, and comparison with a benchmark strategy. A parameterized finite filtration is constructed whose nontrivial statewise distortion agrees exactly with the relative FX settlement multiplier. Hence the resulting filtration--policy model satisfies the bridge $V_*(π^q)=dF(γ)V_*(π^p),$ and, under order compatibility, realizes relative ordinal arbitrage. The remaining problem is to identify the filtration parameters from independent market primitives and to study stability under refinement.

papers.title: Theory of anisotropic magnetotransport beyond the constant relaxation-time approximation in multi-Weyl semimetals
papers.abstract: Multi-Weyl semimetals, characterized by Weyl nodes carrying higher monopole charges, provide a platform for exploring topological magnetotransport beyond the conventional Weyl paradigm. Here, we develop a generalized semiclassical Boltzmann framework for multi-Weyl semimetals with arbitrary monopole charge $N$, incorporating the orbital magnetic moment (OMM) into the quasiparticle dispersion and Berry-curvature-modified dynamics, together with a momentum-dependent collision integral accounting for intra- and intervalley scattering. We investigate the longitudinal magnetoconductivity (LMC) and planar Hall conductivity (PHC) for $N=1$, $2$, and $3$, considering both nonmagnetic and magnetic impurity scattering. In the absence of OMM, the LMC remains positive and quadratic in the magnetic field throughout the investigated scattering regime, consistent with conventional chiral-anomaly-assisted transport. Including OMM, however, leads to a sign reversal of the LMC under sufficiently strong intervalley scattering for the $σ_0$ and $σ_z$ impurity channels. Remarkably, the critical intervalley scattering strength decreases systematically with increasing monopole charge, indicating an enhanced tendency toward negative LMC in higher-charge Weyl systems. Furthermore, we find that the PHC also undergoes a sign reversal for $N=2$ and $N=3$ in the same impurity channels, while remaining positive for $N=1$ within the investigated parameter range. The angular dependences retain their characteristic $\sin^2γ$-like and $\sin2γ$ profiles for LMC and PHC, respectively, even across the sign reversal. Our results demonstrate that the interplay of Berry curvature, OMM, monopole charge, and impurity scattering can produce qualitatively distinct weak-field magnetotransport responses beyond the conventional chiral-anomaly picture.

papers.title: HalluProbe: Exploiting VLM Hallucinations for Backdoor Detection
papers.abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) are vulnerable to backdoor attacks introduced through data poisoning, making effective backdoor detection a critical security challenge. In this paper, we uncover a novel connection between VLM hallucinations and backdoor behaviors and exploit this connection for backdoor detection. Our key insight is that poisoned training data induces strong language priors toward the backdoor target token, while such priors are also a major source of hallucinations. This suggests that enhancing hallucinations can expose hidden backdoor-related priors. Specifically, backdoored VLMs tend to hallucinate backdoor target tokens more frequently across diverse inputs, while the hallucinated tokens of clean VLMs are largely random and exhibit no stable target-specific bias. Based on this observation, we propose HalluProbe, which enhances hallucinations during output decoding and measures the distributional consistency of hallucinated tokens to identify backdoored VLMs. We evaluate HalluProbe against six representative VLM backdoor attacks across three models. Experimental results demonstrate that HalluProbe can effectively detect backdoored VLMs with an accuracy exceeding 90%, outperforming existing backdoor detection methods.

papers.title: Stripped White Dwarfs as Spectroscopic Clocks: Abundance Transitions in Partial Tidal Disruptions
papers.abstract: We investigate partial tidal disruptions of He and CO white dwarfs (WDs) by a $10^{4}\,M_{\odot}$ intermediate-mass black hole (IMBH) using three-dimensional hydrodynamic simulations. We construct realistic WD structures and abundance profiles with MESA and map them into FLASH to follow the remnant response and the time-dependent composition of the fallback debris in single pericentre passages on tightly bound orbits ($e=0.9$). The element-specific fallback rates exhibit pre-peak compositional transitions that trace the WD's stratified layers. In the grazing encounter ($β=0.55$), hydrogen dominates the earliest returning debris, followed by helium, showing a H$\rightarrow$He transition. Deeper encounters ($β=0.7$ and $0.8$) penetrate the CO core and produce a He$\rightarrow$C transition, that occurs earlier relative to peak fallback and is stronger in the deeper encounter. These signatures provide a potential spectroscopic diagnostic for identifying CO-WD tidal disruption events (TDEs). We then develop a semi-analytic model for repeated tidal stripping and predict passage-to-passage compositional evolution, in which the stripped material becomes progressively enriched in heavier elements as deeper layers are exposed, leading to stronger and earlier abundance transitions in later flares. We find that WDs can survive several dozen ($\sim 30$-$80$) passages, depending on their initial mass and compactness. Our results link time-dependent abundance signatures to repeating WD disruptions and provide testable observable predictions for identifying IMBH-powered transients.

papers.title: Uniquely balanced polyhedral complexes are highly connected
papers.abstract: We establish higher connectivity of polyhedral complexes admitting a unique positive balanced top cycle. Our main result shows that, after quotienting by common lineality, every skeleton satisfies the corresponding higher connectivity property. The proof bounds the number of connected components surviving facet deletions by the dimension of the top-cycle space using homological and linear-algebraic arguments. As applications, we prove higher connectivity for all skeleta of arbitrary pointed polyhedral structures on tropical linear spaces of valuated matroids and Bergman fans including nonrealizable cases. These results answer questions raised by Maclagan and Yu.

papers.title: Max-Min Throughput in RSMA-Aided SWIPT for Sustainable Internet of Underground Things: A Deep Reinforcement Learning Approach
papers.abstract: Unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV)-enabled wireless-powered underground sensor networks (WPUSNs) allow underground devices (UDs) to harvest radio-frequency energy from a UAV via wireless energy transfer (WET) techniques, enabling sustainable Internet of underground things (IoUT) applications. This paper integrates rate-splitting multiple access (RSMA)-aided simultaneous wireless information and power transfer (SWIPT) into UAV-enabled WPUSNs to deliver information and energy to UDs. Within this framework, we investigate a max-min fairness problem that jointly optimizes the UAV transmit power, power allocation and message splitting, power-splitting ratios, and time allocation, aiming to maximize the minimum uplink throughput across UDs subject to per-UD downlink throughput requirements and a UAV energy-consumption constraint. To address this non-convex problem under dynamic underground environments, we develop an off-policy deep reinforcement learning approach based on the primal-dual truncated quantile critics (PD-TQC), where a TQC-based reward critic evaluates the fairness objective, cost critics estimate constraint costs, and an actor learns the resource-control policy with adaptive dual-variable updates. Simulations using in-situ soil volumetric water content measurements from a center-pivot irrigation farm demonstrate that PD-TQC achieves the highest annual average minimum uplink throughput compared with four benchmarks while satisfying the per-frame constraints in over 96% of the evaluated frames, and that this throughput advantage is preserved under different Rician factors, numbers of UDs, and downlink throughput thresholds.

papers.title: Local Order Matters: A Lightweight CPU-Trainable CNN for Website Fingerprinting on Defended Tor Traffic
papers.abstract: Website fingerprinting (WF) attacks let a passive adversary infer which site a Tor user visits from the encrypted cell sequence. On undefended traffic, hand-crafted-feature attacks are already near-ceiling, so deep learning offers only a marginal advantage there. We show that the decisive regime is defended traffic: against the FRONT padding defense, which injects dummy cells that corrupt the volume and count features feature attacks rely on, a compact 95,103-parameter 1-D convolutional network trained on the raw cell-direction sequence, on CPU only, stays robust while three implemented direction-only feature baselines degrade. On the closed-world WFlib FRONT set (95 sites), our model reaches 54.2% top-1 accuracy versus 38.5% for the strongest implemented feature baseline (k-FP-style RF), a gain of 15.7 percentage points (3 seeds; seed-0 paired-bootstrap 95% CI [+14.5, +17.0] pp on per-trace correctness, excluding zero). On undefended traffic the CNN reaches 94.1% versus 92.3% for k-FP-style RF. A controlled order-ablation permutes only nonzero traffic cells within each trace, preserving direction counts, retained length, and trailing zero-padding positions while destroying traffic order. This collapses the CNN below every feature baseline (from 54.2% to 7.6%, a 46.6 pp drop), showing that the model depends strongly on order-derived information under FRONT.

papers.title: Velocity weakening and stick-slip in mean-field depinning with stress overshoots
papers.abstract: We study a fully connected depinning model with transient stress overshoots of strength $M$, driven through a spring of stiffness $k_0$. Combining exact stationary relations, linear stability analysis, direct simulations, and population dynamics, we connect the force--velocity characteristic to stick-slip motion and quasistatic avalanche statistics. For $M>1$, two distinct stiffness scales organize the response. At $k_0=k_{\rm w}\equiv M-1$, the stationary characteristic first develops a velocity-weakening branch, whereas $k_0=k_{\rm q}\equiv(M-1)^2/(4M)$ marks the onset of finite-amplitude stick-slip in the quasistatic limit. Their separation produces an intermediate regime in which the quasistatic force converges to a stationary value, whereas finite-velocity driving produces stick-slip below a critical velocity. Quasistatic avalanches in this regime undergo transient amplification and display an excess of large, asymmetric events---"ghost kings"---that remain finite. By contrast, at and below $k_{\rm q}$ the same amplification produces system-spanning "genuine kings" and a finite quasistatic force cycle. These results show how elastic loading dynamically selects among the branches of a reentrant force--velocity relation and clarify the connection between velocity weakening, stick-slip, and runaway avalanches.

papers.title: Bioformer-RetroMAE: retrieval-oriented pretraining of a compact biomedical language model for literature search
papers.abstract: Dense retrieval is increasingly used for biomedical literature search and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). Most biomedical bi-encoders are built on BERTBase-sized encoders pretrained with masked language modeling (MLM). These encoders are costly for corpus-scale indexing and latency-sensitive query encoding, and MLM does not explicitly train the [CLS] vector that a bi-encoder uses to represent a whole text. We present Bioformer-RetroMAE, a compact (43M-parameter) retrieval-oriented biomedical encoder obtained by continually pretraining Bioformer8L} with RetroMAE on approximately 32 million PubMed titles and abstracts. After bi-encoder fine-tuning with BM25 hard negatives, we evaluated it on BioASQ Task 12B test questions by retrieving from all PubMed abstracts. Bioformer-RetroMAE outperformed BioBERT and PubMedBERT bi-encoders fine-tuned under identical settings on all metrics, despite having about 40% of their parameters and producing 512-dimensional rather than 768-dimensional vectors. Compared with PubMedBERT, it improved mean average precision (MAP) by 37.0% and Recall@100 by 29.1%. Compared with the original Bioformer8L}, RetroMAE pretraining improved MAP by 53.6% and Recall@100 by 32.8% without changing model size or inference cost. In hybrid retrieval, fusing Bioformer-RetroMAE with BM25 through weighted reciprocal rank fusion improved MAP and NDCG@10 over BM25 alone by 4.9% and 4.6%, respectively, larger gains than those obtained by fusing BM25 with PubMedBERT or BioBERT.

papers.title: HBF-EventLab: A Discrete-Event Simulator for Studying Host-Device Coordination in High Bandwidth Flash
papers.abstract: High Bandwidth Flash (HBF) combines NAND flash density with high-bandwidth accelerator connectivity, offering additional memory capacity for large language model inference. However, limited hardware availability makes it difficult to evaluate how host behavior and device resource constraints jointly affect HBF request processing. We present HBF-EventLab, an open-source, transaction-level discrete-event simulator based on the Open Compute Project HBF specification. HBF-EventLab connects host request dispatch, command admission, fragmented write assembly, read dispatch, NAND execution, and completion feedback within a shared event loop. It explicitly models distinct resource lifetimes and separates configurable scheduling policies from ordering and resource constraints, enabling controlled exploration of host-device coordination. Experiments show how resource limits, address interleaving, fragment arrival patterns, and scheduling policies affect write completion and request latency. The results highlight the need to consider resource limits and scheduling policies jointly, accounting for their interactions with write assembly and read eligibility. We also integrate HBF-EventLab with real GPU execution of Qwen3-0.6B, combining profiled GPU activity durations with simulated weight-access delays to estimate time to first token and time per output token, with logits and output tokens remaining bitwise identical to those from native GPU execution. HBF-EventLab provides a configurable foundation for studying HBF mechanisms, exploring scheduling policies, and assessing how HBF access delays affect application-level timing. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/sjtu-epcc/HBF-EventLab.

papers.title: Optimisation of gas mixture for charge and light readout with Micromegas detectors
papers.abstract: Optical readout of Micromegas detectors is a promising technique for neutron and charged-particle imaging, offering high spatial resolution while reducing the complexity of electronic readout. Within the framework of the development of optical-readout Micromegas detectors, different noble-gas-based mixtures have been investigated to optimize charge amplification and scintillation yield. Argon-, neon-, and helium-based mixtures with various quenchers were characterized using X-ray irradiation. The detector gain, energy resolution, and optical light intensity were measured simultaneously over a wide range of amplification fields. Unprecedented energy resolutions were achieved over a large detection area (several cm$^2$) with He/\CF and Ne/\CF (90/10) mixtures, reaching 10.5\% and 13.3\% (FWHM), respectively, with the He-based mixture delivering particularly remarkable performance. Simultaneous charge and optical measurements further reveal that high charge gain does not necessarily translate into a strong optical response: while He- and Ne-based mixtures achieve effective charge gains of the order of 10$^5$, Ar/\CF mixtures produce the strongest detected light signals. Among the investigated mixtures, the ternary Ar/\CF/Isobutane (95/3/2) mixture stands out as particularly promising, combining high effective charge gain, a comparatively strong optical response, and more stable detector operation.

papers.title: When Facts Change, Which Decisions Break? Dependency-Aware Context Graphs for Agents
papers.abstract: When an observed fact changes, an agent must identify and repair the decisions that depend on it while preserving unaffected outputs. We investigate the reliability-cost trade-off of field-level dependency graphs extracted from actual agent read traces. A controlled benchmark spans three executable workflow domains and four successive updates, with independent imperative and expression-based references. Across 120 workflows, two models and two repeated runs, we compare full recomputation, rolling summary memory, lexical retrieval, trace-extracted dependencies and verified dependency upper bounds. Trace-derived graphs reduce reviewed decisions and estimated total cost, but omitted alternative supports and missing repair context can reduce complete-plan correctness. Paired ablations isolate the effects of edge deletion, spurious edges, transitive propagation and context scope. An exploratory enhancement supplies the existing record ID/field directory during extraction without revealing unread values or reference edges. We evaluate this enhancement on 60 fresh workflows with two repeats per model. On this fresh set, the directory-aware graph matches observed full-context complete-plan correctness for gpt-6.1-sol (100%) with an estimated 4.0% total-cost reduction, but reaches only 84.8% versus 99.6% for gpt-6-luna. The results distinguish potential dependency impact from actual decision invalidity and show why selective repair must be evaluated with both executable correctness and full memory-processing cost. The evidence concerns explicit procedural workflows; broad real-world agent-memory generalization remains untested.

papers.title: Bridging the Terminology Gap: A Data-Centric Alignment Framework for Multilingual Translation in Cross-Border Corporation
papers.abstract: As globalization accelerates the demand for seamless cross-border enterprise collaboration, multilingual translation remains bottlenecked by insufficient domain-specific terminology, rigid terminology translation, weak instruction-following capabilities, and high inference latency in long-instruction scenarios. To overcome these barriers, we propose Bridging the Terminology Gap (BTG), a data-centric framework. First, BTG mines cross-lingual term alignments from domain documents and leverages LLMs to synthesize terminology-rich parallel corpora. Second, a hybrid filtering strategy combining heuristics and XCOMET scoring ensures high data fidelity. Third, a two-stage training paradigm employs supervised fine-tuning (SFT) for targeted terminology injection, followed by reinforcement learning (RL) to refine output preferences, effectively balancing domain knowledge integration with model reliability. Extensive offline evaluations (e.g., XCOMET, GEMBA, Acc@T) and online human assessments demonstrate significant improvements in terminology accuracy and instruction-following capabilities, validating the effectiveness of our framework, which is now deployed on our cross-border collaboration platform.

papers.title: PanDWM: Panoramic 4D Driving World Models
papers.abstract: Driving world models usually generate videos from six pinhole cameras with separate optical centres and small overlaps, and must learn to keep these views consistent. We present PanDWM, which stitches them into one $360^\circ$ panoramic band. Camera boundaries then fall inside one image, so keeping the views consistent means keeping the image continuous, and each pixel still records its camera ray. Conditioned on layouts, a causal student generates the band window by window in four steps; it is distilled from a causal teacher and trained on its own rollouts. A feed-forward decoder lifts each frame along these rays into 3D Gaussians, and static Gaussians from neighbouring frames complete them into 4D scenes. On nuScenes, scored in one stitched $360^\circ$ view, PanDWM has lower FID and FVD than the multi-camera baselines at $8$-$46\times$ their speed, and keeps its 50-step teacher's FID while lowering FVD by 22-25%.

papers.title: On $ι$Quiver (BPS) Algebras and (Strict) Partitions
papers.abstract: We consider the $ι$quiver algebras of split type associated with the quiver BPS algebras of affine type A. They are supposed to give twisted affine Yangians and (elliptic) $ι$quantum toroidal algebras that could possibly arise from D-branes on $\mathbb{C}\times\mathbb{C}^2/\mathbb{Z}_n$ with orientifolds. We mention some properties of these algebras, such as the minimalistic presentations in the rational cases and the coideal structures. We also investigate how one might identify these algebras from the quiver theories with orientifold actions. Moreover, we discuss some representations with combinatorial bases of these algebras. In particular, the algebras with $n=1,2$ in certain limits of the parameters have representations labelled by (coloured) strict/symmetric partitions, which in the case of $n=1$ recovers the known BPS counting of certain theories.

papers.title: Scaling Fourier Inequalities for Locally Compact Quantum Groups
papers.abstract: In this paper, we study Fourier and convolution inequalities on locally compact quantum groups in the presence of the scaling group. For $1\le p\le 2$, we investigate a family of scaling Fourier transforms and the associated norms $H_{p,θ}(\mathbb G)$, and we show that $H_{p,θ}(\mathbb G)<1$ for the real quantum $az+b$ group and $0<θ<1$, $1<p<2$. We also investigate scaling convolution for locally compact quantum groups and, by extending the ordinary convolution, obtain the corresponding scaling Young inequality in four different regions. In Young Region~II, under $1<p,s<2$ and $2\leq r<\infty$, we construct sequences proving norm one at every effective vertex and prove strict inequality at every other effective point.

papers.title: Indication of demographic and epidemiological data on early-stage risks and long-term epidemic burden
papers.abstract: This study investigates the relationship between age-specific cumulative infection burden and the probability of triggering a major outbreak in heterogeneous populations. We develop two modeling frameworks that incorporate empirical age-stratified contact matrices: a deterministic framework for deriving the final size relation and a stochastic framework based on a Continuous-time Markov chain epidemic model, for which a multi-type branching-process approximation is used to characterize early-stage outbreak risk. The framework is illustrated using empirical social contact data from Guangzhou, Foshan, and Zhuhai, China, under two disease-motivated scenarios representing COVID-19 and hand, foot, and mouth disease (HFMD). The illustrative analyses indicate that the relationship between cumulative infection burden and early-stage outbreak risk depends on both epidemiological characteristics and population contact patterns. In particular, age groups with the highest final attack rates do not necessarily have the highest probability of triggering a major outbreak. These findings highlight the complementary nature of the two measures and the value of considering both when assessing age-specific epidemic risks in practice.

papers.title: Electrical transport of surface-bound electrons on annealed solid neon
papers.abstract: We study the dc transport of electrons bound to the surface of solid neon using the conventional Sommer-Tanner method. First, we find that the capacitive cross-talk for the thickness of solid samples on the order of a millimeter varies substantially with the temperature and is strongly affected by the sample annealing. Second, we find that, even for the annealed samples, the observed response of electrons differs significantly from that of the surface-bound electrons on liquid helium and cannot be satisfactorily described by conventional models. Despite this, we managed to extract the resistance of the electron system from its in-phase response and investigate the temperature dependence in a wide range between 1.4 and 20 K. In a high-temperature range between 16 and 20 K, the resistance behavior is found to agree very well with the vapor-atom scattering mechanism, while at lower temperatures it is consistent with temperature-dependent scattering by surface roughness. Our analysis indicates a high electron mobility of electrons on solid neon but two orders of magnitude lower density than expected. These results suggest surface electrons as a suitable probe for studying the morphology of the neon surface but call for a better understanding of the experimental method applicable to such systems.

papers.title: Sparse Stabilization of Continuous-Time Linear Dynamical Systems
papers.abstract: Efficient use of communication resources is crucial for stabilizing a networked control system. Employing \emph{sparse inputs} and event-triggered control are efficient ways to utilize communication resources in networked control systems. This work considers the problem of stabilizing a continuous-time linear dynamical system (LDS) using $s$-sparse inputs. For this purpose, we consider \emph{switched} linear feedback control, where we construct a finite number of feedback matrices with at most $s$ nonzero rows. Using switched systems theory, we show that there exists an $s$-sparse input for any sparsity level $s \geq 1$ that ensures stability when the continuous-time LDS is stabilizable. In addition, using our approach, we can compute the required feedback matrices with minimal overhead even if the sparsity budget $s$ varies over time. We also minimize the maximum Frobenius norm of the feedback matrices, yielding sparse inputs with reduced control energy. We show that an upper bound on the control energy required for stabilization using an $s$-sparse input is inversely proportional to $s^2$, while maintaining the same exponential stability rate. Finally, we combine the design of the \emph{sparse inputs} with the event-trigger rule to further reduce communication resource consumption. Our sparse and event-triggered control strategy ensures that any stabilizable continuous-time LDS can be stabilized using $s$-sparse inputs under both state feedback and output feedback, for any $s\geq 1$. We illustrate our theoretical results for the task of stabilizing a mass-spring system.

papers.title: Record-proof optical communication enabled by a quantum receiver with lossless optical decryption
papers.abstract: We propose record-proof physical-layer encryption (PLE) based on quantum-optimal reception. Unlike conventional symmetric-key encryption algorithms, the proposed scheme prevents decryption of recorded signals even if the secret key is disclosed after transmission. Existing PLE schemes rely on practical limitations of the eavesdropper's receiver in pursuing record-proof security; ours instead exploits the noncommutativity of conjugate optical quadratures to give the legitimate receiver an intrinsic sensitivity advantage. A phase-controlled Kennedy receiver performs lossless optical decryption and near-optimal binary-state discrimination. We demonstrate record-proof security with a 3.0-dB channel-loss budget, showing that quantum receivers offer cryptographic functions beyond sensitivity enhancement.

papers.title: Sharp Gaussian Approximation for Q-Learning
papers.abstract: Gaussian approximation provides a foundation for online statistical inference in reinforcement learning. We establish sharp non-asymptotic Gaussian approximation rates in Wasserstein distance for asynchronous Q-learning with Polyak-Ruppert averaging. We prove an upper bound of $\widetilde{O}(n^{-1/4})$, where $n$ is the number of iterations, together with a matching lower bound up to logarithmic factors. Q-learning is more challenging to analyze than linear stochastic approximation due to the nonlinearity of the Bellman operator. Asynchronous updates introduce further challenges due to Markovian noise. Our analysis separates the errors from Bellman nonlinearity, Markovian noise, and the finite-sample covariance discrepancy. In particular, we show that Markovian noise induces an unavoidable bias even when the Bellman operator is linear. The trade-off between this bias and the covariance discrepancy determines the convergence rate. We further extend our analysis to the synchronous setting and establish a sharp rate of $\widetilde{O}(n^{-1/2})$.

papers.title: NoLBERT-Calls: Reading Earnings Calls Without Hindsight
papers.abstract: Language models are now a standard tool for measuring what managers say on earnings calls, but the encoders behind these measures were usually pretrained on text from the same years a backtest covers. Holding out a test period does not remove that hindsight, because it sits in the features. We adapt NoLBERT, an encoder pretrained only on text published between 1976 and 1995, to earnings calls without letting it read anything dated after 31 December 2023. The calls supply the training signal themselves: every analyst question is followed by management's answer, and the model learns to pick that answer out from the other answers of the same call. We test on every US call from January 2025 to October 2026 (20,323 calls, 254,575 questions) and make every modeling choice on calls from 2024. The adapted model, NoLBERT-Calls-2023, ranks the true answer first for 78.0% of questions (95% interval 77.8-78.2; chance 8.0%), against 26.3% before adaptation. It is 1.0 point ahead of a call-adapted ChronoBERT, 3.4 points ahead of a call-adapted FinBERT, and 18.7 and 19.8 points ahead of the best off-the-shelf retriever and BM25. A year-by-year test over 2013-2026 finds no look-ahead premium: relative to a model adapted only through 2012, the released model does no better on the years it was trained on than on years it never saw. The price of the cutoff is compute: under one shared 150-minute recipe NoLBERT adapts least well of four encoders, and its lead comes from a longer, staged adaptation of about 13 GPU-hours.

papers.title: A phase diagram for training and inference in language models
papers.abstract: A language model is a complex system whose behavior is determined jointly by the Transformer and the corpus, yet how the representation geometry in the Transformer relates to the actual behavior of language models remains open. We analyze how the representation geometry changes along the forward propagation of actual language models and characterize the representation geometry of a document at a given layer by two collective coordinates, document distinguishability and document dimension. On the phase diagram spanned by these collective coordinates, inference is represented as a flow along depth. We find that, for untrained models, depending on their initialization scale, most of the 156 inference flows move toward the collapse and noise regions of the phase diagram. By contrast, the inference flows of 8 trained models from 5 architecture families all enter and reside in the central region of the phase diagram. Describing the evolution of the flows with a discrete Langevin equation, we find that the difference between the inference flows of untrained runs and those of trained models reduces to whether the effective force on the flows in this region is of saddle or stable-node type. On Pythia-1.4B, we interpret the training process as a phase transition. These results give a unified gateway to the relation between representation geometry and language-model behavior.

papers.title: Reflection Is Not Always Worth It: Budgeted Reflection Allocation for Recommendation Agents
papers.abstract: This work aims to make recommendation agents more efficient by reducing unnecessary LLM reflection while preserving full-catalog ranking and inference reranking. Since BRAVE changes only how training-time reflection is allocated, it does not introduce new user data requirements or additional LLM exposure beyond the base agent protocol. The main potential risk is that a poorly calibrated allocator may assign less reflection to users whose preferences are sparse, niche, or under-represented, which could weaken personalization for those users or indirectly affect item exposure. This risk can be mitigated through deployment-time auditing and conservative allocation design. In practice, reflection budgets should be evaluated not only by aggregate Recall or NDCG, but also across user-history lengths, item popularity groups, and application-relevant cohorts when such analysis is permitted. The allocator should rely on task-side ranking evidence rather than sensitive attributes, and fallback policies can reserve a small portion of the budget for random or fairness-aware coverage when subgroup robustness is important. Privacy risks can be controlled with the same protections required by the base recommendation agent: minimizing user text sent to the LLM controller, anonymizing user identifiers, retaining only necessary interaction evidence, and applying standard access-control and logging policies. Overall, BRAVE is designed as a cost-aware allocation layer, and its ethical deployment depends on validating that the saved computation does not come at the expense of vulnerable users or responsible exposure.

papers.title: Borel $(2n+1)$-coloring for bounded degree function graphs
papers.abstract: Let $G=(X,E)$ be a Borel graph generated by $n$-many bounded-to-one Borel functions. We show that $G$ admits a Borel proper $(2n+1)$-coloring, which answers a problem of Kechris, Solecki and Todorčević.

papers.title: Enhancing Exploration in Ensemble Kalman Inversion via Covariance Inflation and Projected Dropout
papers.abstract: Ensemble Kalman inversion (EKI) is a derivative-free and parallelizable method for parameter estimation in Bayesian inverse problems involving expensive forward models. It adapts Kalman filtering by repeatedly assimilating the observation data through an artificial dynamical system with identity state evolution and the parameter-to-observation map as its observation operator. However, its performance can be limited by ensemble collapse and confinement to the affine span of the initial ensemble. We propose an exploration-enhanced EKI framework that combines multiplicative covariance inflation with a projected-dropout correction of the ensemble mean. Inflation helps maintain ensemble spread, while projected dropout enables the mean to explore directions beyond the initial affine span. For linear inverse problems, we provide a discrete-time, finite-ensemble analysis of the resulting method and prove the least-squares objective converges exponentially to its minimum in expectation. Within the initial ensemble subspace, the contraction factor is independent of the conditioning of the inverse problem, and the limiting ensemble covariance provides a low-rank representation of the posterior covariance. Experiments on ill-conditioned linear systems, 100-dimensional nonlinear benchmarks, and a PDE-constrained barotropic flow inverse problem demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method.

papers.title: A Speech-LLM Framework for Enrollment-Free Wake-Word-Guided Target-Speaker Recognition in Complex Noisy Scenarios for Seamless Human-Machine Interaction
papers.abstract: Target-speaker automatic speech recognition (TS-ASR) is essential for reliable human-machine interaction in complex acoustic environments, where overlapping speech and background noise make it difficult to identify and recognize the intended speaker. Existing approaches typically rely on speaker enrollment or cascaded processing pipelines, limiting their flexibility in practical applications. To address these limitations, we propose an enrollment-free Speech-LLM framework that leverages wake-word text as a lexical cue to guide target-speaker recognition. Specifically, a text-cue encoder extracts lexical representations from the wake word, which are integrated into a pretrained speech encoder through cross-attention to establish an implicit association between the wake-word occurrence and the target speaker. This enables the model to selectively recognize subsequent commands from the target speaker without requiring enrollment speech or explicit wake-word boundaries. Furthermore, a large language model (LLM) unifies command transcription and non-target speaker rejection within a single autoregressive framework. To improve robustness against complex acoustic interference, we develop a large-scale speech synthesis and simulation pipeline with a progressive four-stage training strategy. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed framework achieves a command character error rate of 16.15% and a non-target speaker rejection rate of 91.56%, yielding a unified score of 87.70%, compared with 71.70% for the strongest enrollment-free baseline. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of wake-word-guided speaker selection and highlight the potential of integrating target-speaker recognition and rejection within a unified Speech-LLM framework for robust human-machine interaction.

papers.title: Sangyadhi: An Analytical Framework for Diagnosing and Investigating Collective Care
papers.abstract: While HCI has expanded from Personal to Family Informatics, researchers still lack a critical analytical vocabulary to diagnose what truly constitutes a collective care context. We introduce Sangyadhi, an analytical sociotechnical framework that synthesizes Situated Action, Distributed Cognition, the Capabilities Approach, and Actor-Network Theory to investigate multi-actor care ecologies. The framework articulates four interdependent analytical lenses: contextual grounding, distributed responsibility, trust-mediated sharing, and collaborative actionability. To demonstrate its diagnostic utility, we apply Sangyadhi to critically audit a decade of HCI digital health literature across self-tracking, family informatics, and clinical AI---surfacing structural omissions in how shifting authority, dynamic trust, and AI escalation are conceptualized. Ultimately, the goal of Sangyadhi is to equip researchers with an analytical blueprint for diagnosing observed care contexts, structuring field inquiries, and evaluating future technologies.

papers.title: Splitting of separatrices in generalized standard maps
papers.abstract: We consider generalized standard maps, that is, maps $F_h:(x,y) \mapsto (x+y+f(x;h),y+f(x;h))$ under quite general assumptions. These maps are area preserving. In particular, the Chirikov standard map, the area preserving Hénon map and the case $f(x;h)= \varepsilon(x-x^n)$, $n\ge 2$, where $\varepsilon = 4 \sinh^2(h/2)$ satisfy our hypotheses. For all these cases, the problem of the existence of transverse homoclinic points arises. We prove that, for a wide class of generalized standard maps, the primary homoclinic points are transverse, provided that some constant is different from 0.

papers.title: Asking the right question is key to AI discovery in a chain of hypotheses
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) scientists pursue discovery through a chain of hypotheses, fitting candidate models to existing observations and often choosing experiments where those models disagree most. Yet when early data miss a narrow feature, model selection favors simple curves that agree across the unmea- sured gap, so disagreement-guided search has no reason to look where the new phenomenon lies. When we tested two frontier AI scientists, Claude Sonnet 5.5 and GPT-6.1-Sol, across 32 closed-loop trials with a narrow peak omitted from the starting data, both sampled inside the peak region less often than random search. Surprisingly, the agent that followed model disagreement more closely missed the peak in all 32 trials, whereas discovery succeeded when experiments probed the unmeasured gap early and followed up across the anomaly. Asking the right question, rather than testing only where current models disagree, is therefore key to AI discovery in a chain of hypotheses.

papers.title: Grounding Language Models in Speech Does Not Fix "AI Flavor": Calibrated LLM Judges, Goodhart Traps, and a Preference-Tuning Fix
papers.abstract: Chinese outputs of large language models carry a perceptible "AI flavor": formulaic sentence frames, stacked written-register connectives, repetition loops, and layout leakage. A popular hypothesis blames text-only training for the missing inner-speech layer of human writing; injecting speech or prosody signals should therefore reduce it. We test it with controlled interventions on a 0.6B model; all three fail: (i) phoneme-interleaved continued pretraining yields no spokenness gain under text-matched controls while raising repetition (+0.13 [+0.03, +0.23]); (ii) prosody-plan conditional generation reaches an adherence of only 0.257 against a pre-registered 0.50 gate; (iii) a rule-based reward built on TTS prosody-feature distance is imperceptible in double-blind evaluation by both humans (8/16) and a calibrated LLM judge (9/16). A root cause is evaluation: single-rater blind evaluation at n~20 only detects extreme (>=85%) preferences. We therefore build a calibrated LLM-judge protocol: the judge passes catch trials on known-answer pairs (16/16; single-text 22/24, same-topic pairs 24/24, versus 0.75 for the human rater), then annotates with two independent judges under A/B swapping, counting disagreement as a tie. Using the judge's agree labels directly as DPO pairs (no reward model), we obtain the first positive result: held-out blind win rate 0.833 [0.699, 0.972], repetition 0.114 to 0.000, unchanged MMLU. We further identify a Goodhart channel: the judge's length preference transduces into output-length collapse via pairwise DPO (median 75 chars vs a 300-char prompt); an SFT-anchor repairs it (w is a style knob: w=0.1 preserves gains, w=0.3 does not). Scaling preference data from 89 to 240 pairs yields no additional judge-visible gain. We release RA-Eval v0.1: a three-layer Chinese AI-flavor evaluation framework with 382 judge-annotated preference pairs.

papers.title: Passable for Whom? Few-Shot Personal Calibration of Sidewalk Accessibility Perception
papers.abstract: Whether a sidewalk is passable depends on who is trying to pass: people who use the same mobility aid disagree about the same image, so one label per scene, or per aid, is wrong for many of them. We introduce few-shot personal accessibility perception: from K answers of a person never seen before, predict their judgment of sidewalk scenes never seen before. PassCal separates a shared description of the scene from the person's interpretation of it. The description comes from the internal state of a frozen vision-language model (VLM) and from barrier type, severity and context properties predicted by a detector trained on 14.9k public audits; the interpretation, a calibration of the person's response style and a weighting of the properties, is fit from their answers. On 8,883 judgments in which each of 135 verified mobility-aid users rated the same 50 sidewalk scenes, with people and scenes both held out, eight answers lower the Brier score from 0.550 to 0.479. The same VLM prompted with those answers reaches 0.562, and the same calibration without the scene 0.521. Conformal risk control turns predictions into passable, blocked or "depends on you" statements with a bounded expected rate of wrong statements over people; at 5%, eight answers raise the share of decisive scenes from 27% to 42%. Audit-supervised properties improve all sixteen vision and VLM encoders we test and outperform attributes from a sidewalk navigation VLM.

papers.title: Quantum state tomography with measurement-conditioned diffusion models
papers.abstract: We introduce Diff-QST, a measurement-conditioned diffusion model for quantum state tomography that learns from an ensemble of input states and reconstructs a physical density operator from noisy, possibly incomplete Pauli measurements in two or three denoising steps. In simulations of two to five qubits, Diff-QST has higher mean fidelity than maximum-likelihood estimation (MLE) and a semidefinite-programming least-squares estimator (SDP) in all 120 tested conditions at nominal noise. After training, GPU reconstruction is faster than both in condition-averaged time at every system size and, at four and five qubits, in every condition. At four and five qubits, though not at two and three, Diff-QST also has higher fidelity than an architecture-matched regression baseline trained without diffusion. At five qubits, over the tested numbers of observables and shots per observable, it reaches a specified fidelity with 25%-67% fewer total shots than this baseline. Under state and noise distributions that differ from those used in training, Diff-QST retains its fidelity advantage over MLE and SDP in most tested conditions, although it can reverse. Diff-QST is therefore suited to fast tomography from noisy, incomplete Pauli measurements of states represented by its training ensemble.

papers.title: Counterexamples to Ecker's Conjecture
papers.abstract: Analogous to Perelman's W-entropy defined for Ricci flow, K. Ecker defined a functional W for the mean curvature flow in R^{n+1} and the region it encloses, and made the conjecture that this functional is monotonically increasing in time. In this paper, we give a negative answer to Ecker's conjecture.

papers.title: AGPF: Dynamic Source Selection for Feature Pyramid Fusion
papers.abstract: Feature pyramids provide dense predictors with features at several spatial resolutions. However, it remains largely unexplored which pyramid levels each output location should aggregate information from. We investigate this question by allowing each output location to attend to features from every pyramid level and measuring how attention is distributed across scales. Surprisingly, locations on the finest output grid allocate approximately 75\% of their attention to features two levels coarser, rather than to the current or adjacent levels. Even on the same output grid, the balance shifts toward coarser features as object size increases. These observations motivate Asymmetric Global Pyramid Fusion (AGPF), a neck that preserves the original output grids while allowing each location to dynamically select its contextual sources across scales. Each location interacts with a multiscale memory whose features are aligned in image coordinates, enabling flexible cross-scale aggregation without altering prediction resolutions. Compared with FPN, AGPF improves all 19 object detection and all seven instance segmentation configurations evaluated on COCO. A single fusion block improves Cascade Mask R-CNN by 1.7 box AP and 2.3 mask AP, and the gains consistently transfer to semantic and panoptic segmentation.

papers.title: Saturation and Semi-Saturation Numbers of Joins with Complete Graphs
papers.abstract: For a nonempty family $\mathcal F$ of graphs, a graph is $\mathcal F$-semi-saturated if adding any missing edge creates a copy of some member of $\mathcal F$ containing the added edge, and is $\mathcal F$-saturated if it is also $\mathcal F$-free. The minimum numbers of edges in such graphs of order $n$ are denoted by $\operatorname{ssat}(n,\mathcal F)$ and $\operatorname{sat}(n,\mathcal F)$, respectively. We study these parameters for families of graphs obtained by taking the join of a fixed complete graph with each member of a given graph family. Assume that every member of $\mathcal F$ has at least $8$ vertices, minimum degree at least two, and no triangle containing two vertices of degree two. We give explicit sufficient conditions under which $\operatorname{sat}(n,K_t\vee\mathcal F) =\binom{t}{2}+t(n-t)+\operatorname{sat}(n-t,\mathcal F),$ and characterize all extremal graphs. For the family $\mathcal C_{\ge r}=\{C_\ell:\ell\ge r\}$ of subdivisions of $C_r$, this identity holds for fixed $t\ge1$ and $r\ge4t^2+8t+29$ and all sufficiently large $n$. For $K_t\vee C_k$ with $k\ge2t^2+3t+4$, we establish the corresponding identity for saturation when $n\ge2(k+t-2)^3$ and for semi-saturation when $n\ge56k^3+t-1$.

papers.title: Asymptotics of the three-color Hadwiger-Ramsey numbers
papers.abstract: The Hadwiger-Ramsey number $R_h(k;\ell)$ is defined as the smallest integer $n$ such that for any edge coloring of a complete graph on $n$ vertices in $\ell$ colors at least one of the color classes induces a graph with a $K_k$ minor. We show that $R_h(k;3) = \left(β^{-1} + o(1)\right)k \sqrt{\ln k}$, where $β^{-1} = 2/\sqrt{-\ln(10-4\sqrt6)} = 1.58149\ldots$. This resolves the first open case of a problem by Axenovich and Steiner, who determined the asymptotic behavior of $R_h(k;2)$ and asked about the asymptotics of $R_h(k;\ell)$ for $\ell \geq 3$.

papers.title: Error-correcting codes without parity-check bits
papers.abstract: We are developing a new approach to the problem of error correction in communication channels, in which the input sequence is transformed in such a way that the interdependence of symbols increases significantly. Then, after the sequence is transmitted over the channel, this property is used for error correction, so that the residual error rate is significantly reduced. A natural example of its application is the transmission of binary sequences whose entropy (per symbol) is less than one, since in this case the length of the transmitted sequence remains constant during encoding and decoding. An algorithm has been developed to implement the maximum likelihood method, in which the encoding and decoding times are linear. This algorithm was used to experimentally investigate its effectiveness on popular channel models, and it was found that there are certain sets of parameters for which the proposed method is quite effective.

papers.title: ProTTS: End-to-End Prominence-aware Natural and Controllable Text-to-Speech via Automatic Word Stress Discovery
papers.abstract: Natural speech conveys meaning not only through words, but also through the prominence on a few words. Yet most text-to-speech (TTS) systems remain prominence-unaware, existing prominence-aware TTS require external stress annotations, while unsupervised stress detectors operate in isolation, disconnected from synthesis. This creates a fundamental gap no existing system can automatically discover where stress should be placed, realize it as natural-sounding prosody, and offer user control over emphasis placement, all within a single model. To circumvent this, we propose ProTTS, a unified framework where stress detection emerges from the TTS model itself and, in turn, guides it to synthesize more natural and controllable speech. We incorporate a clustering head into the variance adaptor of FastSpeech_2 that discovers word stress directly from aggregated prosodic features. The discovered stress then drives emphasis variance predictors that modify pitch, energy, and duration for stressed words. The framework is trained end-to-end: TTS reconstruction and clustering losses jointly shape a stress-discriminative feature space without requiring stress labels at any stage. At inference, the same architecture also supports user-controllable emphasis by accepting a custom stress mask. We evaluate ProTTS on ISLE (non-native), LibriTTS, VCTK (native training), and three evaluation benchmarks (Tatoeba, TinyStress-15k, EmphAssess). Listeners prefer ProTTS over the baseline with a MOS of 3.96 vs. 3.12 and 83.5% preference rate. For stress detection, ProTTS achieves 0.839/0.861 F1 on ISLE (German/Italian L2), outperforming unsupervised (0.70) and supervised (0.82) baselines, and 0.933 F1 in zero-shot transfer to Tatoeba.

papers.title: Exploring X17 Couplings through Meson Dalitz Decays
papers.abstract: The ATOMKI collaboration has reported anomalous $e^+e^-$ pair production in a series of nuclear transitions, which has been interpreted as a possible signature of a new light boson, X17. Meson Dalitz decays provide a complementary probe of the X17 interaction structure. However, the widely studied vector coupling scenario is in tension with the combined constraints from existing $D^{*0}\to D^0e^+e^-$, $D_s^{*+}\to D_s^+e^+e^-$ measurements and nuclear transition analyses. In this work, we investigate the X17 contributions to meson Dalitz decays within a framework incorporating both vector and axial-vector couplings, employing the Bethe--Salpeter approach to calculate the hadronic transition matrix elements. With $u$ and $d$ quark couplings taken from previous analyses, we identify allowed regions for the charm and strange quark couplings, which require the axial-vector coupling strength $|g_{c,s}^A|\sim10^{-3}$. We obtain four degenerate best-fit solutions, one of which is $(g_c^V,g_c^A,g_s^V,g_s^A)=(8.32,1.09,-2.62,1.36)\times10^{-3}$, and estimate the decay ratio $R^{\mathrm{th}}(D^{*+}\to D^+e^+e^-)$, which significantly exceeds the Standard Model prediction.

papers.title: Beyond Vehicle-Centric Data: Scaling Autonomous Driving through Roadside-to-Vehicle Generation
papers.abstract: Training autonomous driving models requires large and diverse datasets, collected primarily by vehicles. Scaling them entails investment in fleet operation, data processing and annotation. Road infrastructure records traffic and multi-vehicle interactions, yet the viewpoint gap between roadside and onboard sensors limits its direct use for training. Here we introduce AnyR2V, a framework that transforms multimodal roadside observations into seven-camera surround-view videos for different vehicle perspectives. It aggregates sequential observations into a shared scene representation of geometry and road-user motion, then renders appearance, depth and layout conditions along target-vehicle trajectories. Supervised by spatiotemporally aligned roadside-vehicle pairs, AnyR2V generates surround-view videos guided by scene structure and road-user motion. Existing roadside 3D bounding boxes are transformed into target-vehicle coordinates and paired with generated images, allowing one traffic recording and its annotations to yield training data from multiple vehicle perspectives. We construct R2V360, a dataset of 89 real traffic sequences at an urban intersection, with aligned multimodal roadside data and onboard surround-view videos. AnyR2V outperforms six scene reconstruction methods in image fidelity and in depth and semantic agreement between generated and real onboard images. We further evaluate generated videos along other vehicles' trajectories by adding them to real training data. Adding generated frames equal to 50% of the original real training frame count improves mean average precision (mAP) by 3.3-3.4 AP-points across three 3D object detectors on the real onboard test set, relative to real-data-only baselines. These results demonstrate that roadside traffic records can provide training data from multiple vehicle perspectives, offering a new data source for autonomous driving.

papers.title: Optimal mixing of random-to-random shuffling on linear extensions
papers.abstract: Uniform sampling of linear extensions is a basic problem in randomized algorithms and the study of finite posets. We prove that the random-to-random shuffle of Ayyer, Schilling, and Thiéry mixes in $O(n\log n+n\log(1/\varepsilon))$ steps on every $n$-element poset, establishing their conjectured mixing order. With constant-time order queries, this gives an $\varepsilon$-approximate uniform sampler using $O(n^2(\log n+\log(1/\varepsilon)))$ elementary operations after preprocessing. The proof establishes relative-entropy contraction by a factor $1-1/n$ for the promotion half-step. Consequently, the uniform extended-promotion chain has the same mixing order. We represent complete promotion scans as reflected coordinate paths in the order polytope and prove that a convex potential with gradients in the same polytope has diagonal Hessian mass at most one along each path. Applying this estimate to an optimal transport potential yields a sharp entropy factorization for every finite-entropy input. Linearization also gives the spectral-gap lower bound $(n+1)/n^2$.

papers.title: PRISM: Primitive-Integrated Separable Modulation with Priority Visual Memory Queue for Compositional Zero-Shot Learning
papers.abstract: Compositional Zero-Shot Learning (CZSL) recognizes unseen attribute--object pairs by recombining primitives from seen compositions. Existing methods stop sharing evidence at deployment: fixed prototypes cannot exploit unlabeled test streams, while composition-wise refinement cannot propagate corrections across pairs sharing a primitive. We introduce PRISM, an online CZSL framework that extends primitive sharing to test-time adaptation. Its Hierarchical Knowledge Accumulation Module (HiKAM) factorizes prototype migration into composition-, attribute-, and object-level residual banks. A Priority Visual Memory Queue (PVMQ), initialized by Prototype Queue Initialization (PQI), grounds text updates with bounded visual evidence. The same adaptive core supports exhaustive Full PRISM and recall-calibrated Adaptive PRISM-Lite, which selects candidate budgets from held-out ranks. Comprehensive closed- and open-world experiments on UT-Zappos, MIT-States, and C-GQA demonstrate the state of the art, with Full PRISM achieving the best open-world AUC and harmonic mean on all three benchmarks and the best closed-world results on UT-Zappos and C-GQA. Fine-grained long-tail and non-stationary primitive-block evaluations reveal gains on under-supported concepts and stable adaptation under prolonged skew. Adaptive PRISM-Lite further delivers substantial efficiency gains in the full open-world space with only a small accuracy cost. PRISM thus combines primitive-shared online adaptation, multimodal grounding, and candidate-aware inference.

papers.title: When Does Reusing Layers Help Multimodal Embeddings?
papers.abstract: We ask whether a compact universal multimodal embedding models can produce better search embeddings by running the same layers again. Looped transformers add computation with nearly unchanged model size, making them an appealing alternative to a larger encoder. Their success in language-model reasoning and recent use for retrieval motivate the idea, but higher retrieval scores alone do not reveal what an extra pass contributes. We study eleven loop designs and training variants on three checkpoints of one vision-language architecture. Our protocol distinguishes whether a model uses its extra pass, whether its image states respond to the query, and whether those updates improve retrieval. We prove that an image placed before the query remains query-independent through repeated layers when information only travels forward. We then open a query-to-image path in three ways, including order-alternating recurrence, which places the query first on the next pass. Each path produces query-sensitive image states. For bidirectional attention and order alternation, freezing later visual updates does not lower accuracy. On all 78 datasets of the Massive Multimodal Embedding Benchmark version 2 (MMEB-V2), a standard added loop loses 0.46 points against its trained control; an intermediate generative stage changes the effect to +0.36. A model pretrained with recurrence gains +4.23 points over its own loop-removed control and benefits from query-conditioned image updates when answering visual questions or locating objects from text.

papers.title: Where Is Rank-1 DiM Refusal Intervenable in Multimodal LM Derivatives?
papers.abstract: Open-weight model hubs now ship not only chat checkpoints but a long tail of derivatives---fine-tunes, safety guards, vision--language models (VLMs), audio wrappers, and generative heads---yet residual-stream safety audits still often intervene at a single site, usually the text decoder $T$. We ask a localization question under one shared mean / rank-1 difference-in-means (DiM) extract$=$intervene protocol, with matched-norm random and empty-rate controls: does causal chat attack lift concentrate at $T$, or do perceptual encoders, projectors, and fusion paths ($E$/$P$/$F$) supply a comparable bypass? On the mixed-input settings we stress-test---HADES adversarial images paired with harmful text prompts, and spoken AdvBench via text-to-speech (TTS) or silence---text DiM at $T$ raises attack success rate (ASR) while the same mean DiM at $E$/$P$/$F$ does not; attacks track harmful text rather than image or audio content. Margin-rank and leverage probes on a Vision leaf show that this recipe is extremal at $T$ and near chance at $P$/$E$, which pressures a weak-extractor reading of those flat cells for the DiM family we study. Catalog breadth and mapper-free base$\to$derivative transfer when residual widths match provide supporting coverage under the same gates; generative U-Nets are a separate band under generation judges. The primary claim is this recipe-scoped $T$ vs.\ non-text intervenability asymmetry---intervention accessibility under mean / rank-1 DiM, not a claim that refusal is absent or fully represented outside $T$ (text vs.\ perceptual contrasts and pooling differ by site). On VLGuard Unsafe prompts ($n{=}200$; Llama-Guard), the same $T$ vs.\ $P$/$E$ directionality holds at modest absolute ASR ($0.030{\to}0.150$ at $T$). An intervention-oriented Class$\times$site ledger records where this protocol still hooks as supporting coverage, not as a universal multimodal bypass.

papers.title: Foundation Pareto Flow Policy for Multi-Objective Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: The overarching goal of reinforcement learning (RL) is to efficiently optimize the agent's policy for various environments, tasks, dynamics, and even user preferences, which often consist of multiple and potentially conflicting rewards/objectives. This necessitates the learning of Pareto-optimal policies that can navigate different trade-offs among objectives. However, existing multi-objective RL (MORL) methods, whether trained online or offline, are typically limited to task- or objective-specific policy learning and do not address generalization of learned trade-offs to unseen tasks/objectives. In this work, we propose the Foundation Pareto Flow Policy (FP2) for offline MORL in continuous robotic control, inspired by the pre-mid-post-training paradigm underlying recent foundation models. Specifically, we instantiate FP2 as a multi-modal diffusion transformer equipped with a likelihood-free flow matching loss, enabling unified, scalable, and instructable learning of diverse trade-off trajectories. We further develop a three-stage training pipeline to gradually optimize the policy: (1) pre-training on a large-scale MORL dataset, (2) mid-training on a carefully curated high-quality dataset, and (3) post-training on few collected trajectory data from new tasks and trade-offs. Empirical results demonstrate that FP2 outperforms previous state-of-the-art methods on most tasks of the D4MORL benchmark, achieving superior zero-shot interpolation and extrapolation on complex Pareto manifolds as well as efficient few-shot adaptation of the learned trade-off prior to new continuous-control tasks. Code is available at https://github.com/FibonacciRabbit/FP2.

papers.title: The Erdős similarity problem for polynomials and analytic maps
papers.abstract: In this paper, we study the Erdős similarity problem by replacing affine copies with images of polynomial maps or analytic maps. This is inspired by a connection between a partial converse of Szemerédi's theorem and the Erdős similarity problem and its variants, as well as a version of polynomial Szemerédi's theorem by Bergelson and Leibman. In particular, we strengthen several known results in the literature. We show that a large class of sequence are not polynomially universal in this sense. First, for sequences satisfying suitable gap hypotheses, an explicit Cantor-type witness is constructed. Second, for sets satisfying certain growth conditions, a random Cantor-type witness is constructed, extending work of Kolountzakis. This also extends certain results in recent work of Cuéllar-Iosevich-Kulkarni-Aravena-Yavicoli to the polynomial setting. Finally, we show for arbitrary sequences $A$ with zero as an accumulation point that the $(d+3)$-fold sumset $(d+3)A$ is not polynomially universal when restricted to polynomials of degree at most $d$; this complements classical work of Bourgain.

papers.title: EfficientSkill: Learning Skills for Token-Efficient Multi-Turn Agents
papers.abstract: Reflective skill optimizers improve multi-turn LLM agents by revising instructions from failed and successful rollouts, yet accumulating edge-case rules bloats prompts, inflates token use, and pushes agents into long, error-prone loops.
