At the adopted field, broad Hamming-space spreading coexists with a strong preference for low-energy states. This regime follows a sharp increase in displacement as the field is raised. To connect this behaviour to the landscape, a short-time expansion relates the onset of escape to target distance and intermediate energies. Bounds on isotropic spin flips and on the free transverse mixer quantify the role of the Bernasconi potential in the observed transfer. At N = 28, the ground-state probability at t = 30 exceeds a canonical cost prediction fitted to the same mean energy by a factor of about 1.9. The cost of generating each quantum sample is assessed separately through a hardware estimate, which places a direct circuit implementation two to three orders of magnitude beyond present processor capabilities.

papers.title: Inelastic confinement-induced resonances in multiwell potentials
papers.abstract: Recently, resonance features associated with multiwell effects have been reported in a fascinating experiment conducted with an ultracold-atom quantum simulator [Y. K. Lee, H. Lin, and W. Ketterle, Phys. Rev. Lett. 131, 213001 (2023)]. The results were explained as a consequence of superexchange, which determines the spin dynamics in a singly-occupied Mott insulator, by allowing for the virtual population of two particles on the same site. In this work, a complementary interpretation of the resonance features is provided based on inelastic confinement-induced resonances, manifested as avoided crossings in the two-particle spectrum, showing excellent agreement with the experimental results. The comparison of the results of the single- and double-well descriptions of the optical trapping potential confirms the multiwell origin of the experimental features. However, the double-well model is already shown to be sufficient for providing an explanation of the apparent symmetry violation that occurs within single-well models. Furthermore, certain limitations of the harmonic approximation are discussed.

papers.title: Staged Semantic Distillation: Preserving Free-Form Semantics in a Low-Compute Non-LLM Surrogate of a Staged LLM Agent
papers.abstract: Staged LLM agents make market and social simulators realistic, but one 102-day run of a 200-agent, ten-index market simulator issues 203,100 language-model calls and returns one realization. Conventional low-compute distillation drops their free-form intermediate state. We present staged semantic distillation, a low-compute method that preserves non-structured semantics in a non-LLM student trained from one recorded trace. A frozen encoder maps each teacher output to a 1024-d vector; the student sees typed stage-tagged vectors with stage-specific visibility, is jointly supervised, and trains with scheduled self-history. One TwinMarket trace yields a 13.2M-parameter deterministic student that trains in 1,658 seconds on one 8-GB GPU and runs with zero teacher or decoder calls and no text generation (0.14 ms per decision). Its analysis stays close to the teacher (cosine 0.943), and swapping semantic inputs between agents moves 64.7% of decisions against 12.8% for a matched donor, so the channel is preserved and live. We use the surrogate to study what the transfer carries. It reaches 0.8347 balanced accuracy on the teacher-forced replay and 0.7783 [0.766,0.791] on the deployment decoder; the five-seed gain over a no-semantic retrain is +2.2 [1.21,3.14]. Against the teacher's own re-sampling level, round-one R is 97.1% [95.8,98.4] and 92.3% [89.0,95.4]; R is a diagnostic, not an accuracy. A five-seed content-by-schedule study isolates the gain: scheduled self-history carries it (+2.2 [1.21,3.14]); shuffled and constant content controls reproduce it, while content matters teacher-forced. The design rule: invest in the deployment schedule, let content earn its place at the teacher-forced operating point. A 20-seed, 200,000-decision sweep takes 12 minutes with zero LLM calls, versus three hours for the teacher. The paper is a method-and-case-study contribution on one simulator and trace.

papers.title: NetBreaker: Benchmarking Network Dismantling across Objectives, Scales, and Toplogoies
papers.abstract: Network dismantling seeks to fragment a network with as few node removals as possible, which is widely applied in vulnerability analysis, epidemic containment, and infrastructure protection. Although learning-based methods have become increasingly prominent, their progress remains difficult to assess because existing studies differ in method coverage, datasets, evaluation criteria, and experimental protocols. Thus, we introduce NetBreaker, a comprehensive benchmark designed for the learning era of network dismantling. NetBreaker organizes 30 methods (18 non-learning and 12 learning-based) under a common taxonomy and evaluates them on 185 networks from eight unified domains, ranging from 14 to 1.69 million nodes. To enable fair comparison, heterogeneous method outputs are converted into node removal sequences and assessed under a unified execution protocol. The evaluation covers four complementary dimensions: target-based effectiveness, trajectory-based effectiveness, structural diagnostics, and applicability & computational efficiency. Extensive experiments show that current learningbased methods do not consistently outperform strong non-learning approaches, while exposing substantial differences in effectiveness, scalability, and efficiency across network conditions and evaluation perspectives. NetBreaker provides a reproducible basis for measuring progress and developing reliable, scalable, and computationally efficient network dismantling methods.

papers.title: Where Mixture Recognition Fails: An Ingredient-Level Audit of Unseen Combinations in SmellNet
papers.abstract: An electronic nose must name every ingredient of a mixture, including combinations it has never measured. SmellNet, a public benchmark for this task, scores ingredients with a hit rate that is told how many each sample contains. We audit what this protocol hides. We hold out ingredient combinations from the SmellNet training data, evaluate four architectures (MLP, CNN, LSTM and a Transformer encoder) without revealing the ingredient count, and repeat the evaluation once on the official unseen split. Under the count-informed protocol, 90-96% of mixtures receive an ingredient that is absent, on our folds and on the official split alike. On our folds, every model identifies one ingredient reliably but the second rarely, and it completes the pair with a familiar training partner about twice as often as chance. On the official split, even the first-ranked ingredient is correct in only 29-46% of binary mixtures, often because a frequent training ingredient that is absent from every test pair is ranked first, and on its combinations that are truly absent from training no model names both ingredients in more than 1.2% of them. The failures fall on the same ingredients for every architecture, and a frequency correction only moves errors between ingredients. Mixture recognition is therefore limited by ingredients the models cannot separate and by a preference for frequent ingredients, not by the architecture, and it should be evaluated with set-level errors and without oracle cardinality.

papers.title: Predicting local electric field in Al$_x$Ga$_{1-x}$N p-i-n photodiodes using exciton Franz-Keldysh photocurrent spectroscopy
papers.abstract: In AlGaN p-i-n photodiodes, reverse bias redshifts and broadens the sub-bandgap photocurrent responsivity through the eXciton Franz-Keldysh (XFK) effect, and this spectral line shape encodes the local electric field inside the device. Fitting the photocurrent spectra of two such photodiodes, with 5% and 40% Al, to an XFK absorption model at each bias yields the local voltage, $V_l$, a single parameter that sets the line shape and uniquely determines the electric-field profile inside the device. In both devices, $V_l$ varies linearly with the applied bias ($R^2 = 0.994$ and $0.998$) but changes far more slowly than the bias itself, revealing a strong local reduction of the electric field that points to non-uniform electrostatics. The slopes show that only 12.4% of the applied bias in the 5% Al device, and 45.8% in the 40% Al device, drops across the junction at the probed location. Extrapolated to zero bias, $V_l$ gives built-in voltages of 3.39 and 4.29 V, within 0.02 V of the 3.41 and 4.28 V obtained from technology computer-aided design (TCAD) simulation, which validates the extracted local voltages at equilibrium. These results extend sub-bandgap photocurrent spectroscopy to AlGaN devices as an optical probe of local electrostatics, relevant to ultraviolet photodetectors and high-voltage electronics.

papers.title: Optional Traps: An Empirical Study of LLM Agents Against Credential Deception and Alert-Driven Revocation
papers.abstract: Deception (honeypots, decoys and canary credentials) rests on a simple premise: legitimate users never touch a fake asset, so any touch is a high-confidence signal. We ask whether that premise holds when the attacker is a large language model (LLM) agent, and what deception contributes once ordinary hardening is in place. We built an isolated, hash-chained lab around a mock Records API and report four studies. (1) In an exploratory run, a local 9.7B-parameter model ignored every optional decoy, read a genuinely leaked service key from a debug endpoint and exported the protected records in both static and adaptive deception modes. (2) After removing the leak, planting a canary credential in its place and revoking the offending client, a frozen 60-session study with a 4B-parameter model found export success of 20/20 at baseline, 0/20 with hardening alone and 0/20 with hardening plus deception (exact paired McNemar p = 1.9e-6 baseline vs. defended; p = 1 hardened vs. defended). Deception added detection and per-client revocation in 19 of 20 defended sessions, but no measurable prevention beyond hardening. (3) On Google Cloud, a real OpenCanary login alert was authenticated, signed and turned into revocation of the attacking client; the first denied export followed within an observed upper bound of 303 ms, a separate legitimate client completed 100/100 requests, and all 14 control checks passed. (4) In multi-agent swarm engagements, agents that used the canary were revoked 39-59 s after the bait was served without affecting siblings, but one model-driven legitimate agent also took the bait, a false-positive risk specific to LLM clients. Against LLM agents, traps must sit on the attacker's path rather than beside it, closing real weaknesses does the preventive work, and deception's measurable value is fast, attributable detection. All results are lab-scale and are not a production claim.

papers.title: Initial Conditions Dictate Gas-Stellar Counter-Rotation in Galaxies
papers.abstract: We present a physical origin of gas-stellar counter-rotation in galaxies. Scale-dependent partitions of tidal torques from cosmic primordial perturbations source angular momentum for distinct baryonic components. This scale dependence maps to radial hierarchy in Lagrangian space clustering: stellar components, assembled at earlier times from the inner protohalo, retain persistent memory of small-scale tidal torques, whereas gas, accreted later from outer Lagrangian regions, is governed by large-scale perturbations and can develop counter-rotation. This mechanism is observationally testable and offers a direct probe of the hierarchical cold dark matter (CDM) paradigm. Unlike conventional late-time scenarios that only explain the existence of counter-rotation, our framework further predicts its component-resolved direction, enabling component-resolved angular momentum to serve as a new probe of primordial density perturbations and improving cosmological initial condition reconstruction.

papers.title: Bayesian Time-Varying Spectral Estimation for LISA with P-Splines
papers.abstract: We model the evolutionary spectrum of a slowly time-varying process by a linear combination of products of time- and frequency-dependent B-splines, placing a Gaussian tensor-product penalty prior on the coefficients. The posterior distribution is obtained by updating the prior using a Whittle-type likelihood approximation of the Wilson-Daubechies-Meyer time-frequency coefficients. Separate regularisation in time and frequency allows non-stationary spectral structure to be inferred. An adaptive coarse-grained likelihood reduces the computational cost while preserving fine resolution around sharp spectral features. We first validate the method using repeated simulations of a locally stationary process with known spectrum, showing lower reconstruction errors and narrower posterior intervals as the sample size increases. We then apply it to a year-long simulated LISA data set with stationary instrumental single link spectra, an evolving time-delay interferometry (TDI) response, and a modulated Galactic foreground. We compare a flexible total power spectral density (PSD) model with models incorporating progressively stronger physical information and examine both continuous and gapped observations. Allowing time variation substantially improves reconstruction relative to a stationary model, while incorporating physical information about the TDI response further improves recovery, particularly near its moving spectral features. The results illustrate the trade-off between spectral flexibility, physical assumptions, and posterior uncertainty in non-stationary LISA noise estimation.

papers.title: Complete Hypergraph States as a Resource for Robust Quantum Metrology
papers.abstract: Hypergraph states extend graph states by incorporating many-body interactions via multi-controlled-$Z$ gates, but their metrological advantages and design principles remain elusive. We develop an analytical expression for the quantum Fisher information (QFI) of complete weighted hypergraphs with respect to the collective-spin generators $J_x$ and $J_y$, reducing to three finite binomial averages requiring $O(n|K|)$ arithmetic for a set of hyperedge orders $K$. At the entangling phase $ϕ=π$, order-optimized $J_x$ sensing approaches the Heisenberg limit (HL), while $J_y$ oscillates between the HL and half the HL at large total number of qubits, $n$. We derive the quadratic and linear coefficients of the QFI under erasure and dephasing noise, showing that complete hypergraph states retain Heisenberg scaling for finite erased particles and dephasing probability $p<0.5$ in the asymptotic system size limit. For $J_y$ sensing, computational basis measurement, or, more simply, using Hamming weight detection, is sufficient to saturate the QFI under noiseless conditions and retain Heisenberg scaling under both noises. These results suggest that complete hypergraphs are a robust resource for practical metrological sensing tasks.

papers.title: Spreads Don't Price a Rival Market Maker's Information
papers.abstract: When one market maker becomes better informed, do its competitors widen their bid-ask spreads? Adverse-selection reasoning suggests that they should, because the better-informed maker avoids toxic order flow and leaves more of it to the others, and the closest model of competition with an informed dealer predicts more conservative quotes by the uninformed dealers. We study this question in a stochastic quoting game in which one maker receives a private signal of varying precision about a persistent state that drives order flow. Strategies are learned with independent reinforcement learning, which we benchmark against an exact dynamic-programming solution of the single-agent case. In none of the configurations we examine does the average spread of the uninformed makers increase with the rival's precision. Where competition for order flow is weak, the slope of their spread in precision is statistically equivalent to zero within half an action tick; where competition is strong, their spread tightens. The informed maker's own spread tightens markedly in every configuration and serves as a positive control. These results hold with two, three and four makers, across an eightfold variation in the depth of the background liquidity, with a background quote that reprices after toxic fills, and under price-time priority. Our measurements point to a competitive trade-off. In the model the total toxicity of the flow does not depend on any maker's information. A better-informed maker avoids more of it, and where this leaves more toxic flow to its competitors, it also quotes more tightly, so that a wider quote would cost them more order flow than it would save in adverse selection. The uninformed makers adjust the skew of their quotes and their inventory instead, and the rival's information changes the distribution of profits across makers while quoted spreads remain nearly unchanged.

papers.title: An all-steps-at-once algorithm for time-domain wave propagation in heterogeneous and unbounded media
papers.abstract: We propose, analyze, and implement a convolution quadrature (CQ) algorithm for transient acoustic waves in an unbounded medium consisting of a heterogeneous domain embedded in free space, where the wave speed may be spatially variable and discontinuous. Multistep CQ, applied to the time-domain solution operator, reduces the evolution problem to a family of Helmholtz problems with damped complex frequencies, which can be solved independently in parallel, all time steps at once. The frequency problems are discretized by an overlapping coupling of finite elements (FEM) on a polygonal/polyhedral domain containing the inhomogeneity, and boundary elements (BEM) on a smooth curve enclosed by that domain, in the region where the medium is homogeneous, which accounts exactly for the unbounded exterior. Neither discretization needs to conform to the geometry of the heterogeneous domain, nor to each other. For the resulting FEM--BEM coupling we prove bounds for the solution operators of the transformed problems that are explicit in the Laplace parameter and the wave speed. These bounds yield convergence of the time discretization for A-stable multistep schemes. We also prove explicit estimates on the exponential decay of the transformed solutions away from the heterogeneity, which show that the correction provided by the BEM part is small but relevant, and cheap to compute: a few GMRES iterations suffice, and the correction is needed only over a fixed range of weakly damped frequencies, beyond which it becomes negligible and can be dropped. Numerical experiments confirm the predicted convergence rates in time and space and explore iterative (multigrid) methods for the interior FEM problems.

papers.title: VLN-Flash: Parallel Action Decoding with Adaptive Execution for Vision-and-Language Navigation
papers.abstract: When a vision-and-language navigation policy generates an action sequence autoregressively, the robot waits for a chain of dependent predictions. A small discrete action vocabulary makes it possible to score all short-horizon plans in parallel. We introduce VLN-Flash, a training-free decoder that evaluates the complete action-prefix tree in a single forward pass. Branch-specific attention and matched token positions preserve the original policy's conditional action distribution for each prefix in exact arithmetic. We use the score margin between the stepwise-greedy prefix and its strongest alternative at each depth to decide how many actions to execute. The robot then executes the plan with the highest joint score at the chosen depth before observing again. On matched inputs, VLN-Flash achieves a nearly $3\times$ speedup in action decoding over native autoregression on Uni-NaVid and StreamVLN. Compared with the native autoregressive decoders, it improves success rate and success weighted by path length (SPL) on R2R-CE and RxR-CE, with success gains up to 2.7 percentage points. On a Unitree GO2, VLN-Flash improves navigation success and cuts the mean wait between actions by about 160 ms after subtracting network transmission time.

papers.title: On Representational and Functional Alignment of Training Data Attribution Methods for Language Models
papers.abstract: Existing approaches to training data attribution derive influence estimates from different sources of information, including gradients, model-internal states, and surface-level similarity. However, comparisons between attribution methods remain incomplete, often relying on indirect evaluations through downstream task performance. In this work, we introduce a framework for directly comparing methods along three dimensions: functional alignment, which measures correlation between full attribution vectors; representational alignment, which captures structural similarity of the representations underlying attribution; and cross-method predictability, which evaluates agreement on local pairwise ranking decisions. We observe strong representational and moderate functional alignment within paradigms. Alignment across paradigms is low and task-dependent, yet stable across models. Our results suggest that the similar downstream performance observed across paradigms in prior work can be attributed to agreement on the relative importance of documents, rather than to agreement on rankings of the full training data.

papers.title: Generate, Align, and Restore: MLLM-Empowered Diffusion for Generalizable Low-light Image Enhancement
papers.abstract: Low-light image enhancement (LLIE) is essential to numerous vision applications operating under adverse illumination. Despite substantial advances, real-world nighttime enhancement remains challenging due to the scarcity of strictly aligned day-night pairs and complex degradations involving extreme darkness and heterogeneous artificial light sources, leading to fragile generalization. To overcome these challenges, we propose MrLIE (MLLM-empowered reference Low-light Image Enhancement), a novel reference-based unsupervised LLIE framework that synergizes the generative and reasoning capabilities of multimodal large language models (MLLMs) with conditional diffusion. MrLIE employs the MLLM as a high-fidelity reference synthesizer and diagnostic critic, iteratively generating, diagnosing, and correcting normal-light references directly from degraded nighttime observations. Based on this, our method governs the enhancement process through two complementary mechanisms, in which a confidence offset module rectifies spatial-geometric inconsistencies for reference reliability and a structure-anchored injection scheme harmonizes aligned reference cues, low-light structural constraints, and ControlNet additive anchoring during the denoising process. Extensive experiments on diverse benchmarks demonstrate that MrLIE achieves superior perceptual quality, natural appearance, and robust generalization.

papers.title: LC-ISP Benchmark: Learning Advanced ISP with Live and Capture Streams
papers.abstract: High-quality paired RAW-to-sRGB datasets are essential for data-driven ISP, yet existing datasets often rely on cross-device collection, causing misalignment and failing to faithfully reflect real capture conditions. We therefore introduce LC-ISP, a large-scale benchmark built from the intrinsic gap between a camera's live preview and offline capture streams. LC-ISP contains 53.9k spatially aligned groups, each comprising live RAW/live sRGB and multi-frame fused RGB/capture sRGB, and covers day, night, indoor, outdoor, and HDR scenes. It also provides capture-stream intermediates for modular supervision. We further develop a compact two-stage baseline that uses these intermediates as auxiliary targets. Under a 2.5-GFLOP budget for 448$\times$448 RAW inputs, it outperforms the strongest single-frame baseline by over 2 dB PSNR while improving texture, denoising, and color reproduction. LC-ISP supports realistic benchmarking, the design of supervision strategies, and the development of lightweight ISP models.

papers.title: Fourier Crosstalk and Leakage Correction for Binary-Encoded Fourier Single-Pixel Imaging
papers.abstract: Digital micromirror devices enable high-speed Fourier single-pixel imaging (Fourier-SPI), but their binary modulation introduces quantization errors that degrade the reconstructed image quality. In particular, each binarized Fourier probe contains non-target Fourier components, thereby distorting the corresponding Fourier-domain measurement. This Letter presents a Fourier domain correction framework that characterizes these errors using the Fourier-domain response matrix of the decoded binary Fourier patterns. Accordingly, a response-matrix-based Fourier-SPI measurement model is established by partitioning the matrix into components associated with the sampled and unsampled frequencies, thereby decomposing the quantization error into sampled-frequency crosstalk and unsampled-frequency leakage. This model established a generalized correction framework, termed Fourier Crosstalk and Leakage Correction (FCLC), alongside two simplified methods: Fourier Sampled-Frequency Crosstalk Correction (FSCC) and Fourier DC Crosstalk Correction (FDCC). FSCC is implemented via an inversion-free Richardson-type iteration, whereas FDCC admits a closed-form solution. Numerical simulations and experiments across multiple binary encoding strategies reveal that the proposed framework improves reconstruction fidelity without modifying the binary patterns or acquisition process.
